short: Trajan pushed Roman power to Mesopotamia's furthest extent, only for his gains to unravel at once.
full:
In 113 CE, Trajan marched east on the pretext of a disputed Armenian succession, annexing Armenia as a province in 114 and then advancing down the Tigris and Euphrates into Mesopotamia. By 116 he had captured the Parthian capital Ctesiphon and reportedly sailed the Persian Gulf, extending Roman territory further east than it would ever again reach and creating the short-lived provinces of Mesopotamia and Assyria.

The conquest proved impossible to hold. Widespread Jewish revolts across the eastern Mediterranean and North Africa (the Kitos War) and Parthian-backed uprisings in the newly won territory forced Trajan into costly reconquest even as his health failed. He died in August 117 before returning to Rome, and his successor Hadrian abandoned the new eastern provinces almost immediately, restoring the Euphrates as the practical frontier.
